title: 150 Years of Return Predictability Around the World: A Holistic View

extraction.methodology_summary: The paper tests return predictability using payout-price ratios (coupon-price, dividend-price, and rent-price) across long-term government bonds, equities, and housing markets in 16 developed countries from the 1870s to 2020. Predictive OLS regressions and expanding out-of-sample moving windows are performed to evaluate statistical significance, out-of-sample R-squared, and economic utility gains (certainty equivalent return) for mean-variance investors, alongside vector autoregression (VAR) simulations for payout growth.
extraction.universe: 16 developed countries covering long-term government bonds, equities, and housing markets, as well as representative agents' risky and wealth portfolios.

performance_metrics.evidence_quote: Given the transaction costs, ex., commission alone can be as high as 6% in the US, whether timing the housing market with rent growth can be economically meaningful — even for the most promising market, i.e., the Finnish housing market with 0.61% CER gain — remains a question.

key_findings: None of the 48 country-asset combinations show consistent in-sample and out-of-sample performance with a positive utility gain for mean-variance investors.
Out-of-sample predictability is virtually absent for bond markets, while only isolated equity and housing markets show predictive power.
Predictive regressions based on Cochrane's VAR analysis show that 14 countries have predictable dividend growth and 5 countries have predictable rent growth in their respective markets.
VAR simulations do not reject the null hypothesis that returns are not predictable, nor do they reject that dividend growth is predictable across international data.
limitations: High transaction costs (such as real estate commissions and turnover expenses) can easily eliminate small certainty equivalent return gains.
Data availability and sample period lengths vary across countries.
